questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (scene safety, violence)
questions.q: You arrive at a residence for an assault call and see a person holding a knife in the front yard. Law enforcement has not arrived. What should you do?
options: Approach calmly and ask the person to drop the knife
Enter through the back door to reach the patient
Park in front of the house with emergency lights on
Stage at a safe distance until police secure the scene
questions.explain: An EMT does not enter a scene that is not safe. Staging out of sight at a safe distance and waiting for law enforcement protects the crew so they remain able to treat patients. Trying to disarm someone is outside the EMT role.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (standard precautions)
questions.q: What is the minimum standard precaution an EMT should take before touching any patient?
options: Wearing an N95 respirator
Wearing a full-length gown
Wearing disposable gloves
Wearing a full face shield
questions.explain: Gloves are the baseline protection for any patient contact because blood and body fluids may be present. Additional protection, such as eye protection, a mask or a gown, is added when splashes or airborne disease are likely.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (standard precautions, airborne disease)
questions.q: You are called for a patient with a productive cough, night sweats and weight loss over several weeks. Which respiratory protection should you wear?
options: No mask if gloves are worn
A loose cloth face covering
A fit-tested N95 respirator
A paper dust mask
questions.explain: These findings suggest tuberculosis, which spreads by airborne particles. An N95 or higher respirator protects the EMT. A surgical mask may be placed on the patient to limit spread, but cloth and dust masks do not protect the provider.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (scene hazards, electrical)
questions.q: A car has struck a utility pole and a power line is lying across the hood. The driver is conscious. What should you do?
options: Move the line off with a dry wooden broom
Help the driver step out of the car
Stay clear and tell the driver to remain inside
Touch the car briefly to test for current
questions.explain: A downed line may be energized, and anyone touching the car and the ground at the same time can be electrocuted. The safe zone is set well back, the driver is told to stay in the vehicle, and the utility company or trained crews handle the line.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (hazardous materials awareness, positioning)
questions.q: You approach an overturned tanker truck with a placard and a liquid leaking onto the road. Where should you position the ambulance?
options: Uphill and upwind at a safe distance
Downhill so any runoff is easy to see
Downwind to keep vapors behind you
Next to the tanker to block traffic
questions.explain: Hazardous vapors and liquids move with the wind and flow downhill, so staying upwind and uphill at a distance limits exposure. The EMT reads the placard number from afar, for example with binoculars, and consults the Emergency Response Guidebook.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (hazardous materials awareness, reference guide)
questions.q: At a hazardous materials scene, what is the Emergency Response Guidebook used for?
options: Finding initial actions from the placard number
Recording vital signs for each patient
Calculating doses of rescue medications
Assigning triage colors to patients
questions.explain: The Emergency Response Guidebook links UN identification numbers and material names to guides that describe hazards, isolation distances and initial actions. It helps awareness-level responders keep themselves and others safe until a hazmat team arrives.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (mechanism of injury, frontal impact)
questions.q: An unrestrained driver hit a tree head-on, and the steering wheel is bent. Which injury should you suspect?
options: Isolated injury to the lower back
Burn injury to both hands
Sprain of the right ankle only
Chest injury from striking the wheel
questions.explain: A deformed steering wheel shows the driver's chest struck it with great force, so chest and abdominal injuries, including to the heart, lungs and liver, are suspected. The mechanism raises the index of suspicion even before signs appear.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (mechanism of injury, windshield damage)
questions.q: A front-seat passenger in a head-on crash has a starred windshield in front of her. Which injuries should you suspect?
options: Head and cervical spine injuries
Hand and wrist fractures only
Isolated injuries to the feet
Minor abrasions of the shins
questions.explain: A star or spider-web pattern in the glass means the head struck it. Head injury and injury to the cervical spine are suspected, so the EMT watches mental status closely and considers spinal motion restriction.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (number of patients, additional resources)
questions.q: While sizing up a two-car crash, you count four patients and your unit has two EMTs. When should you request more resources?
options: After treating the most injured patient
Now, before starting patient care
After loading the first patient
Once you reach the receiving hospital
questions.explain: Requesting additional units during size-up, before becoming committed to one patient, gets help moving early. Once an EMT starts care it is easy to delay the call, and the other patients wait longer for help.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (START triage, walking wounded)
questions.q: Using START triage, how are patients who can walk to a designated area categorized?
options: Immediate, tagged red
Delayed, tagged yellow
Minor, tagged green
Expectant, tagged black
questions.explain: In START, patients who can follow directions and walk are tagged green, or minor, and assessed again later. This quickly separates them so rescuers can focus on patients who cannot move. Walking patients can still get worse, so they are reassessed.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (START triage, apneic adult)
questions.q: During START triage, an adult is not breathing. You reposition the airway and the patient still does not breathe. How do you tag this patient?
options: Immediate, red
Delayed, yellow
Minor, green
Expectant or deceased, black
questions.explain: In adult START triage, a patient who does not breathe after the airway is repositioned is tagged black. Resources go to patients who can survive with care. If breathing starts after repositioning, the patient is tagged immediate.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (START triage, respiratory rate)
questions.q: During START triage, an adult who cannot walk is breathing 36 times per minute. What category is this patient?
options: Delayed, yellow
Immediate, red
Minor, green
Expectant, black
questions.explain: In START, a respiratory rate above 30 breaths per minute places an adult in the immediate category. Patients breathing 30 or fewer times per minute move on to a perfusion check and then a mental status check.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (START triage, perfusion)
questions.q: During START triage, an adult is breathing 22 times per minute but has no radial pulse. How should you tag this patient?
options: Delayed, yellow
Immediate, red
Minor, green
Expectant, black
questions.explain: An absent radial pulse, or capillary refill longer than 2 seconds, shows poor perfusion and makes the patient immediate in START. The rescuer may quickly control major bleeding before moving on. A normal breathing rate alone does not place the patient in the delayed group.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (START triage, mental status)
questions.q: During START triage, an adult who cannot walk has a respiratory rate of 18, a radial pulse and follows simple commands. What tag applies?
options: Immediate, red
Delayed, yellow
Minor, green
Expectant, black
questions.explain: An adult who cannot walk but breathes 30 or fewer times per minute, has a radial pulse and follows commands is placed in the delayed group. Failing to follow commands would make the patient immediate, and being able to walk would make the patient minor.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (JumpSTART pediatric triage)
questions.q: Using JumpSTART triage, a child is not breathing after airway positioning but has a palpable pulse. What should the rescuer do?
options: Tag the child black and move on
Start full CPR at that location
Tag the child green to treat later
Give five rescue breaths, then reassess
questions.explain: JumpSTART recognizes that children often stop breathing from respiratory causes before the heart stops. An apneic child with a pulse gets five rescue breaths. If breathing resumes, the child is tagged immediate; if not, the child is tagged expectant.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (scene hazards, carbon monoxide)
questions.q: You respond to a home where three family members all have headaches and nausea. A fuel-burning space heater is running. What should you suspect and do first?
options: Carbon monoxide; get everyone out of the home
Food poisoning; collect samples of the meal
Influenza; put masks on everyone inside
Migraine; dim the lights and treat inside
questions.explain: Several people with the same headache and nausea in a building with a fuel-burning heater suggests carbon monoxide. The priority is to move everyone, including the crew, to fresh air and request fire department air monitoring. Pulse oximetry can read falsely normal in this poisoning.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (crime scene awareness)
questions.q: You are treating a gunshot victim at a crime scene. Which action helps preserve evidence?
options: Cutting clothing around, not through, the bullet holes
Moving the weapon into the ambulance for police
Cleaning the blood off the floor before police arrive
Throwing the cut clothing into a nearby trash bin
questions.explain: Patient care comes first, but EMTs avoid disturbing evidence. Cutting around holes in clothing, leaving items where they were found, bagging clothing for police and noting what was moved all help investigators. Touching weapons or cleaning the scene destroys evidence.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (scene safety, escalating scene)
questions.q: While you treat a patient at a domestic dispute, the partner begins shouting threats and blocking the door. What should you do?
options: Argue back firmly to take control of the room
Leave with the patient if possible and call police
Continue your exam and ignore the threats
Restrain the partner until help arrives
questions.explain: A scene that becomes unsafe calls for retreat to safety and help from law enforcement. The EMT's safety comes first, and arguing or restraining the person increases the danger. Care can resume once the scene is secured.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (mechanism of injury, lateral impact)
questions.q: A car was struck on the driver's door by another vehicle. Where should you expect most of the driver's injuries?
options: Only to the lower legs
Mostly to the right side
Only to the face and jaw
On the left side of the body
questions.explain: In a lateral impact, the occupant on the struck side absorbs the force directly, so injuries to the head, neck, chest, pelvis and arm on that side are common. In the United States the driver sits on the left, so the left side of the body is most at risk.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (mechanism of injury, rollover)
questions.q: Why is a rollover crash considered a high-risk mechanism of injury?
options: Vehicles that roll over seldom have airbags
Rollovers happen only at very low speeds
Occupants can be struck from many directions
Seat belts stop working once a vehicle rolls
questions.explain: In a rollover, occupants are thrown in several directions and may strike many surfaces or be ejected, so injury patterns are unpredictable. EMTs keep a high index of suspicion for serious injury, especially when an occupant was unrestrained.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (mechanism of injury, ejection)
questions.q: A motorcyclist was thrown from the bike and landed about 30 feet away. How does this mechanism affect your assessment?
options: Assume minor injuries because a helmet was worn
Check only the limbs that struck the pavement
Suspect serious injuries even if few signs are visible
Delay the assessment until the bike is moved
questions.explain: Ejection transfers large forces to the body and is linked with severe injury. A helmet protects the head but not the chest, abdomen or spine. A rapid full-body assessment is done and the patient is treated as a high priority.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (mechanism of injury, penetrating trauma)
questions.q: A patient was stabbed once in the upper abdomen with a kitchen knife. What does this mechanism suggest?
options: Injury is limited to the skin surface
An exit wound will always be present
Organs beneath the wound may be injured
Internal bleeding is rare with knives
questions.explain: Low-velocity penetrating injury damages tissue along the path of the blade, so organs such as the liver, stomach or spleen beneath the wound may be injured. External bleeding may be small even when internal bleeding is serious.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (mechanism of injury, blast)
questions.q: After an explosion, which organs are most at risk from the primary blast pressure wave?
options: Air-filled organs such as the lungs and ears
Solid bones such as the femur and pelvis
The skin of the hands and the forearms
The large muscles of the thighs and back
questions.explain: The primary blast wave affects hollow, air-filled organs, so lung, ear and bowel injuries can occur even without visible wounds. Flying debris and being thrown by the blast cause the secondary and tertiary injuries, such as fractures and penetrating wounds.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (roadway safety, apparatus placement)
questions.q: Fire apparatus is blocking the lane behind a crash on a highway. Where should the ambulance park?
options: Upstream, behind the fire apparatus
Alongside the wreck in the next lane
In the median facing oncoming traffic
Downstream, past the crash scene
questions.explain: When fire apparatus blocks traffic upstream, the ambulance parks downstream of the crash, inside the protected area, so patients can be loaded safely and the unit can leave without being boxed in. Parking beside the wreck exposes the crew to passing traffic.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (roadway safety, visibility)
questions.q: When working at a roadway incident, which item increases an EMT's visibility to drivers?
options: A dark navy uniform jacket
A pair of safety glasses
A high-visibility safety vest
A pair of leather gloves
questions.explain: Being struck by vehicles is a leading danger at roadway scenes. A reflective, high-visibility vest makes responders easier to see by day and at night. Dark clothing blends into the surroundings, and glasses or gloves protect the wearer but do not improve visibility.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (scene hazards, animals)
questions.q: You arrive at a home and a large dog is growling at the door. What should you do?
options: Walk past the dog quickly and confidently
Spray the dog with water from a bottle
Enter through a window instead of the door
Ask the owner to secure the dog before entering
questions.explain: Animals are a scene hazard. The EMT asks that the animal be secured in another room, or requests animal control or police. Rushing past an aggressive dog risks bites to the crew, who then cannot help anyone.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (nature of illness)
questions.q: On a medical call, which source helps you determine the nature of illness during scene size-up?
options: The patient's health insurance card
Information from the patient, family or bystanders
The weather report for that day
The number of cars parked on the street
questions.explain: The nature of illness is gathered from what the patient, family and bystanders say, plus scene clues such as medication bottles, home oxygen or odors. It guides the assessment much as the mechanism of injury guides a trauma assessment.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Scene Size-Up and Safety (hazardous atmospheres, confined space)
questions.q: Several workers in a factory collapse near a tank. A coworker runs in to help and also collapses. What should you do?
options: Stay out and call for hazmat resources
Go in quickly while holding your breath
Enter wearing a surgical mask and gloves
Pull the nearest worker out by the arms
questions.explain: Several people collapsing in one area, including a rescuer, signals a toxic or oxygen-poor atmosphere. Entering without proper training and breathing apparatus only adds victims. The EMT isolates the area, denies entry and requests specialized resources.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (general impression)
questions.q: What is the first step of the primary assessment once the scene is safe?
options: Take a full set of vital signs
Obtain a SAMPLE history
Perform a head-to-toe exam
Form a general impression of the patient
questions.explain: The primary assessment begins with a general impression: age, sex, level of distress and whether the patient looks sick. It is followed by checking responsiveness, airway, breathing and circulation. Vital signs and history come later, after life threats are managed.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (responsiveness, AVPU)
questions.q: A patient does not respond to your voice but moans and pulls away when you pinch the trapezius muscle. How is the patient described using AVPU?
options: Alert
Responds to verbal stimuli
Unresponsive
Responds to painful stimuli
questions.explain: In AVPU, P means the patient responds only to a painful stimulus. V would mean a response to voice, and U means no response at all. Any level below alert is a reason to watch the airway closely.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (responsiveness, AVPU)
questions.q: A patient keeps her eyes closed but opens them and answers when you speak loudly. How do you describe her on the AVPU scale?
options: Alert
Responds to verbal stimuli
Responds to painful stimuli
Unresponsive
questions.explain: A patient who reacts only when spoken to is at the V level. An alert patient has the eyes open and interacts without prompting. Recording the AVPU level allows later changes to be noticed.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway management, trauma)
questions.q: An unresponsive patient fell from a ladder. Which technique should you use to open the airway?
options: Head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver
Neck extension with a pillow
Jaw-thrust maneuver
Rolling the patient face down
questions.explain: The jaw-thrust opens the airway while keeping the head and neck in line, which is preferred when spinal injury is suspected. If the jaw-thrust does not open the airway, opening the airway takes priority and the head-tilt, chin-lift is used.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway management, medical patient)
questions.q: An adult is found unresponsive in bed with no sign of trauma. Which method should you use to open the airway?
options: Head-tilt, chin-lift
Abdominal thrusts
Back blows
Chest thrusts
questions.explain: Without suspected trauma, the head-tilt, chin-lift is the simplest and most effective way to lift the tongue away from the back of the throat. Abdominal thrusts, chest thrusts and back blows are used for foreign body obstruction, not routine airway opening.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway adjuncts, OPA sizing)
questions.q: How is an oropharyngeal airway sized?
options: From the tip of the nose to the chin
From the corner of the mouth to the earlobe
From the chin to the sternal notch
From the lips to the eyebrow
questions.explain: The correct oropharyngeal airway reaches from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe or the angle of the jaw. An airway that is too long can push the epiglottis over the opening of the airway, and one that is too short can push the tongue back.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway adjuncts, OPA contraindication)
questions.q: You insert an oral airway into an unresponsive patient, and the patient begins to gag. What should you do?
options: Push it in further to get past the gag
Tape it in place and keep ventilating
Replace it with a larger oral airway
Remove the airway and have suction ready
questions.explain: A gag reflex means the patient can partly protect the airway, and an oral airway can trigger vomiting and aspiration. It is removed, suction is kept ready, and a nasopharyngeal airway may be considered instead.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway adjuncts, NPA sizing)
questions.q: How is a nasopharyngeal airway sized?
options: From the corner of the mouth to the chin
From the tip of the nose to the earlobe
From the nose to the sternal notch
From the earlobe to the collarbone
questions.explain: The nasopharyngeal airway length matches the distance from the tip of the nose to the earlobe, and its diameter should fit the nostril. It is lubricated with a water-soluble lubricant before insertion.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway adjuncts, NPA contraindication)
questions.q: Which finding is a reason not to insert a nasopharyngeal airway?
options: An intact gag reflex in a drowsy patient
Snoring respirations in an overdose patient
Clear fluid draining from the nose after head trauma
Clenched teeth during a seizure
questions.explain: Clear fluid from the nose after head trauma may be cerebrospinal fluid from a skull fracture, and the airway could pass into the skull. Nasopharyngeal airways are tolerated by patients with a gag reflex and are useful when the teeth are clenched.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway adjuncts, NPA insertion)
questions.q: When inserting a nasopharyngeal airway into the right nostril, which way should the bevel face?
options: Toward the outer nostril wall
Toward the upper lip
Toward the forehead
Toward the nasal septum
questions.explain: The bevel faces the septum, the wall between the nostrils, so the tip slides along it without catching tissue. Using a lubricated airway and gentle insertion straight back along the floor of the nose reduces bleeding.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (suction, adult)
questions.q: What is the maximum time to suction an adult's airway in a single attempt?
options: 30 seconds
45 seconds
15 seconds
60 seconds
questions.explain: Suction removes oxygen along with secretions, so adult attempts are limited to about 15 seconds, with shorter times for children and infants. The patient is oxygenated or ventilated between attempts.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (suction, infant)
questions.q: How long should a single suction attempt last for an infant?
options: About 15 seconds
About 5 seconds
About 20 seconds
About 30 seconds
questions.explain: Infants have small oxygen reserves and become hypoxic quickly, and suctioning can slow the heart rate. EMT teaching limits infant suction attempts to about 5 seconds, compared with about 10 seconds for children and 15 seconds for adults.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (suction, technique)
questions.q: When suctioning the mouth with a rigid tip, how far should it be inserted?
options: Down into the trachea
Only as far as you can see
Until the patient gags
Past the vocal cords
questions.explain: The rigid tip goes only where the EMT can see it, usually not beyond the base of the tongue, to avoid injuring tissue or triggering vomiting and a slow heart rate. Suction is applied while the tip is withdrawn.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway sounds, gurgling)
questions.q: An unresponsive patient has gurgling sounds with each breath. What should you do first?
options: Insert an oral airway
Apply a nasal cannula
Check the blood glucose
Suction the airway
questions.explain: Gurgling means fluid is in the upper airway, and it must be cleared before ventilation or adjuncts are used. Inserting an airway or ventilating first can push secretions deeper and cause aspiration.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway sounds, snoring)
questions.q: An unresponsive patient's breathing sounds like snoring. What is the most likely cause?
options: Fluid in the lower airways
The tongue partly blocking the airway
Spasm of the small airways
A collapsed lung on one side
questions.explain: Snoring respirations come from the tongue and soft tissue falling back into the upper airway. Repositioning the head and jaw or inserting an airway adjunct usually corrects it. Fluid causes gurgling, and small-airway spasm causes wheezing.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway sounds, stridor in a child)
questions.q: A child makes a harsh, high-pitched sound when breathing in. What does this sound indicate?
options: Fluid in the small air sacs
Normal breathing for a child
Narrowing of the upper airway
Spasm of the lower airways
questions.explain: Stridor is a harsh, high-pitched sound, usually on inhalation, caused by partial obstruction or swelling of the upper airway, as with croup or a foreign body. Wheezing points to narrowing of the lower airways. A child with stridor is kept calm in a position of comfort.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (oxygen devices, nonrebreather)
questions.q: At what flow rate should a nonrebreather mask be set for an adult?
options: 10 to 15 liters per minute
1 to 2 liters per minute
4 to 6 liters per minute
20 to 25 liters per minute
questions.explain: A nonrebreather needs 10 to 15 L/min so the reservoir bag stays inflated during inhalation and delivers a high concentration of oxygen. With too little flow the bag collapses and the patient may not get enough air.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (oxygen devices, nasal cannula)
questions.q: What is the usual flow range for a nasal cannula?
options: 1 to 6 liters per minute
10 to 15 liters per minute
8 to 12 liters per minute
15 to 25 liters per minute
questions.explain: A nasal cannula delivers low-concentration oxygen at 1 to 6 L/min. Higher flows dry and irritate the nose without adding much oxygen. It suits patients with mild hypoxia or those who cannot tolerate a mask.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (oxygen administration, indications)
questions.q: According to current AHA guidance, what is appropriate for a patient with chest pain who is alert, breathing normally and has an oxygen saturation of 98 percent on room air?
options: Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min
Begin ventilations with a BVM
Withhold supplemental oxygen and monitor
Apply a nasal cannula at 6 L/min
questions.explain: Current AHA guidance does not recommend routine oxygen for suspected acute coronary syndrome when the saturation is normal and there is no respiratory distress. Oxygen is given when the saturation is low or the patient shows hypoxia or breathing difficulty.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (ventilation, adult with a pulse)
questions.q: An adult has a pulse but is not breathing adequately. How often should you ventilate with a bag-valve mask?
options: One breath every 6 seconds
One breath every 2 seconds
One breath every 12 seconds
One breath every 15 seconds
questions.explain: For an adult with a pulse who needs ventilation, about one breath every 6 seconds, or 10 breaths per minute, is given. Each breath lasts about 1 second and just makes the chest rise. Faster rates cause stomach inflation and reduce blood return to the heart.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (ventilation, infant with a pulse)
questions.q: An infant has a pulse but is breathing inadequately. At what rate should you give rescue breaths?
options: One breath every 6 to 8 seconds
One breath every 10 seconds
One breath every 2 to 3 seconds
One breath every 15 seconds
questions.explain: Current AHA guidance for infants and children with a pulse who need rescue breathing is one breath every 2 to 3 seconds, or 20 to 30 breaths per minute. Children use oxygen faster and need a higher ventilation rate than adults.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (CPR, advanced airway)
questions.q: During adult CPR, an advanced airway is in place. How should ventilations be given?
options: Two breaths after every 30 compressions
One breath every 2 seconds without pausing
One breath every 6 seconds with continuous compressions
Two breaths after every 15 compressions
questions.explain: With an advanced airway, compressions continue without pauses and a breath is given about every 6 seconds. The 30 to 2 ratio applies to adults without an advanced airway. Overventilation reduces blood flow back to the heart.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (CPR, pediatric ratio)
questions.q: Two rescuers are performing CPR on a 6-year-old. What compression to ventilation ratio should they use?
options: 30 compressions to 2 breaths
15 compressions to 2 breaths
5 compressions to 1 breath
3 compressions to 1 breath
questions.explain: For children and infants with two rescuers, the ratio is 15 to 2. A single rescuer uses 30 to 2 for all ages beyond the newborn period. The 3 to 1 ratio is used for newborns just after birth.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (CPR, compression rate)
questions.q: What compression rate is recommended during CPR?
options: 100 to 120 per minute
60 to 80 per minute
80 to 100 per minute
120 to 150 per minute
questions.explain: High-quality CPR uses a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Slower rates produce less blood flow, and faster rates reduce depth and leave too little time for the heart to refill between compressions.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (CPR, adult compression depth)
questions.q: How deep should chest compressions be for an adult?
options: At least 2 inches but not more than 2.4 inches
About 1 inch, to avoid any rib fractures
About 1.5 inches, the same as for an infant
At least 3 inches, for adequate blood flow
questions.explain: Adult compressions should be at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep but not more than 2.4 inches (6 cm), with full chest recoil after each one. Shallow compressions do not move enough blood, and excessive depth increases injury.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (CPR, infant compression depth)
questions.q: How deep should chest compressions be for an infant?
options: About 1.5 inches, one third of chest depth
About 0.5 inch, one tenth of chest depth
About 2.5 inches, half of chest depth
About 3 inches, the same as an adult
questions.explain: Infant compressions are about one third of the front-to-back depth of the chest, which is about 1.5 inches (4 cm). For children it is about 2 inches. Compressions that are too shallow give little blood flow.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (CPR, infant technique)
questions.q: Two rescuers are performing CPR on an infant. Which compression technique is recommended?
options: Heels of both hands on the lower sternum
One closed fist on the upper sternum
Two fingers placed over the xiphoid
Two thumbs with the hands encircling the chest
questions.explain: The two thumb-encircling hands technique produces better depth and blood flow and is recommended when two rescuers are present. Compressions are on the lower half of the sternum, just below the nipple line, and never over the xiphoid process.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (AED, early use)
questions.q: You arrive at an adult in cardiac arrest with an AED while your partner performs CPR. What should you do first with the AED?
options: Check a pulse for 30 seconds
Give two breaths before using it
Turn it on and attach the pads
Wait for paramedics to arrive
questions.explain: Early defibrillation improves survival in shockable rhythms, so the AED is turned on and the pads applied as soon as it arrives, while CPR continues until the device analyzes. Long pulse checks delay both compressions and shocks.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (AED, analysis)
questions.q: The AED announces that it is analyzing the heart rhythm. What should the rescuers do?
options: Continue compressions during the analysis
Give two breaths while it is analyzing
Check for a pulse at the wrist
Pause compressions and not touch the patient
questions.explain: Movement from compressions or touching the patient can interfere with rhythm analysis. Everyone clears the patient, and CPR resumes right after a shock is delivered or a no-shock message is given.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (AED, pediatric use)
questions.q: You are using an AED on a 4-year-old in cardiac arrest, but pediatric pads are not available. What should you do?
options: Skip the AED and continue CPR alone
Use adult pads, making sure they do not touch
Cut the adult pads to a smaller size
Use one adult pad on the chest only
questions.explain: For children under 8, pediatric pads or a dose attenuator are preferred. When they are not available, adult pads are used, placed front and back if needed so they do not touch. A shock through adult pads is better than no defibrillation.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (circulation, pulse check)
questions.q: How long should a rescuer take to check for a pulse in an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally?
options: No more than 10 seconds
At least 20 seconds
About 30 seconds
A full 60 seconds
questions.explain: Pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds so compressions are not delayed. If a definite pulse is not felt within that time in an unresponsive patient who is not breathing normally, CPR is started.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (circulation, infant pulse)
questions.q: Where should you check the pulse of an unresponsive infant?
options: The carotid artery in the neck
The radial artery at the wrist
The brachial artery in the upper arm
The pedal pulse on top of the foot
questions.explain: An infant's short, chubby neck makes the carotid pulse hard to find, so the brachial artery on the inside of the upper arm is used. For children, the carotid or femoral pulse is checked.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (breathing assessment, agonal breathing)
questions.q: An unresponsive adult is taking occasional gasping breaths and has no pulse. What should you do?
options: Apply a nonrebreather mask
Place the patient on the side
Begin chest compressions
Wait to see if breathing improves
questions.explain: Occasional gasps, called agonal breathing, are not effective breathing and are common early in cardiac arrest. A pulseless, unresponsive patient with only gasping needs CPR right away. Oxygen by mask does not help a patient who is not moving air.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (breathing assessment, inadequate breathing)
questions.q: A patient who took an unknown amount of pills is breathing 6 times per minute with shallow chest rise. What is the priority?
options: Apply a nasal cannula at 4 L/min
Obtain a full list of medications
Assist ventilations with a bag-valve mask
Place the patient on the side and observe
questions.explain: A rate of 6 with shallow breaths does not move enough air, so ventilation is assisted with a BVM and oxygen. A cannula or mask needs adequate breathing to work. The history is gathered after the airway and breathing are managed.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (bleeding control, direct pressure)
questions.q: A patient has steady dark red bleeding from a cut on the forearm. What should you do first?
options: Apply a tourniquet above the elbow
Apply firm direct pressure to the wound
Raise the arm and wait before pressure
Place a cold pack on the forearm
questions.explain: Most external bleeding stops with firm direct pressure. A tourniquet is used for life-threatening limb bleeding that direct pressure does not control, or when pressure cannot be applied. Elevation alone is not a reliable way to control bleeding.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (bleeding control, tourniquet placement)
questions.q: Direct pressure fails to control severe bleeding from a lower leg wound. Where should the tourniquet be applied?
options: Directly over the wound itself
Just below the wound, toward the foot
Over the knee joint for a firmer hold
2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint
questions.explain: A tourniquet is placed 2 to 3 inches above the wound, avoiding joints, and tightened until the bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone. If the wound location is unclear, it is placed high on the limb.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (bleeding control, tourniquet care)
questions.q: After applying a tourniquet that stopped the bleeding, what should the EMT do?
options: Loosen it every 10 minutes
Note the time and leave it in place
Hide it under clothing for warmth
Remove it once the bleeding slows
questions.explain: Once applied, a tourniquet is left in place and loosened only by hospital staff. The time of application is written down and reported, and the tourniquet stays visible. Loosening it can restart heavy bleeding.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (bleeding control, junctional wounds)
questions.q: A patient has severe bleeding from a deep wound in the groin where a tourniquet cannot be applied. What should you do?
options: Pack the wound and hold firm direct pressure
Apply a tourniquet around the waist
Cover it lightly and transport quickly
Raise the leg and apply an ice pack
questions.explain: Junctional wounds, such as in the groin or armpit, cannot be controlled with a limb tourniquet. Packing the wound tightly with gauze, hemostatic if available, and holding firm pressure is the accepted approach. A light covering does not stop arterial bleeding.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (bleeding, types)
questions.q: Which description fits arterial bleeding?
options: Dark red blood flowing steadily
Slow oozing from small vessels
Clear fluid weeping from the skin
Bright red blood spurting with the pulse
questions.explain: Arterial blood is rich in oxygen, so it is bright red, and it spurts in time with the heartbeat because it is under high pressure. Venous bleeding is darker and flows steadily, while capillary bleeding oozes slowly.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (shock, early signs)
questions.q: Which finding is an early sign of shock in an adult?
options: Low blood pressure
Fixed, dilated pupils
Absent radial pulses
Anxiety and a rapid pulse
questions.explain: Early in shock, the body compensates by raising the heart rate and narrowing blood vessels, and reduced brain perfusion causes restlessness or anxiety. Falling blood pressure and loss of peripheral pulses are late signs that compensation is failing.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (shock, pediatric considerations)
questions.q: Why is blood pressure an unreliable early sign of shock in children?
options: Children have higher pressure than adults
Children maintain pressure until shock is advanced
Blood pressure cannot be measured in children
Children rarely lose enough blood to drop it
questions.explain: Children compensate well by increasing heart rate and narrowing vessels, so blood pressure stays near normal until a large share of blood volume is lost. A fast heart rate, delayed capillary refill and mottled skin are earlier signs. Low blood pressure in a child is an ominous late finding.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (shock, treatment)
questions.q: A trauma patient has cool, pale skin and a rapid, weak pulse. Which action is appropriate?
options: Give sips of water to replace lost fluid
Keep the patient warm and transport promptly
Have the patient walk to the ambulance
Stay on scene until the pulse slows down
questions.explain: Shock care at the EMT level includes controlling bleeding, giving oxygen as needed, keeping the patient supine and warm, and rapid transport. Nothing is given by mouth because surgery may be needed, and walking increases oxygen demand.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (circulation, capillary refill in a child)
questions.q: In a 3-year-old, capillary refill takes 4 seconds. What does this suggest?
options: Poor perfusion, a possible sign of shock
Normal circulation for a toddler
Fever without any circulation problem
Good hydration and normal perfusion
questions.explain: In infants and young children, capillary refill longer than about 2 seconds suggests poor perfusion. Combined with a fast heart rate or cool skin, it points to shock. Cold surroundings can also slow refill, so it is interpreted together with other findings.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (priority and transport decisions)
questions.q: Which patient is a high priority for rapid transport?
options: An alert patient with a minor ankle injury
An unresponsive patient with no gag reflex
A patient with a small cut on one hand
An alert patient with a mild headache
questions.explain: Unresponsiveness and loss of the gag reflex mean the patient cannot protect the airway and may be getting worse. Such patients need immediate airway management and prompt transport. The other patients are stable and lower priority.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (priority and transport decisions, trauma)
questions.q: A trauma patient is unresponsive and shows signs of shock. What is the goal for on-scene time?
options: Stay at least 30 minutes to stabilize
Finish a detailed exam before leaving
Wait until all splints are applied
Keep it short, ideally 10 minutes or less
questions.explain: Critical trauma patients often need surgery that cannot be done in the field. The aim is to treat immediate life threats and keep scene time to about 10 minutes or less. Detailed exams and splinting of minor injuries are done during transport if time allows.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (breathing, open chest wound)
questions.q: A patient has a stab wound to the chest with air bubbling from it. What should you do?
options: Pack the wound with dry gauze
Leave it open so air can escape
Cover it with a moist dressing
Cover it with an occlusive dressing
questions.explain: An open chest wound lets air enter the chest, so it is sealed quickly with an occlusive dressing or vented chest seal. The patient is watched for signs of tension pneumothorax, and the dressing is lifted briefly to release pressure if breathing worsens.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway management, infant positioning)
questions.q: How can you keep an unresponsive infant's airway in a neutral position on a flat surface?
options: Place a thick pillow under the head
Tilt the head back as far as possible
Place a thin pad under the shoulders
Turn the head fully to one side
questions.explain: An infant's large back of the head pushes the chin toward the chest when lying flat, which can block the airway. A thin pad under the shoulders brings the airway to a neutral position. Overextending the neck can also block the soft infant airway.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway obstruction, infant)
questions.q: A responsive infant is choking and cannot cry or cough. What should you do?
options: Give abdominal thrusts until it clears
Give 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts
Sweep the mouth blindly with a finger
Hold the infant upside down by the feet
questions.explain: For a responsive infant with a severe obstruction, repeated cycles of 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts are used. Abdominal thrusts can injure an infant's liver, and blind finger sweeps may push the object deeper.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway obstruction, adult becomes unresponsive)
questions.q: An adult who was choking becomes unresponsive. What should you do?
options: Keep giving abdominal thrusts while standing
Do blind finger sweeps before anything else
Start CPR and look in the mouth before breaths
Give back blows with the patient on the floor
questions.explain: When a choking adult becomes unresponsive, the rescuer lowers the patient and starts CPR, since compressions may dislodge the object. Each time the airway is opened for breaths, the rescuer looks in the mouth and removes a visible object. Blind sweeps are avoided.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway obstruction, pregnancy)
questions.q: A woman who is 8 months pregnant is choking and cannot speak. Which maneuver should you use?
options: Abdominal thrusts
Chest thrusts
Back slaps alone
Blind finger sweeps
questions.explain: Chest thrusts are used in late pregnancy, and in patients so large the rescuer cannot reach around the abdomen. Abdominal thrusts could harm the uterus and fetus. Back slaps alone are not the standard adult technique.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (OB, supine hypotension)
questions.q: A woman in her third trimester becomes dizzy and pale while lying flat on her back. What should you do?
options: Raise her legs and keep her flat
Turn her onto her left side
Have her stand and walk around
Place her head lower than her feet
questions.explain: In late pregnancy, the uterus can press on the inferior vena cava when the woman lies on her back, reducing blood return to the heart and lowering blood pressure. Turning her to the left side moves the uterus off the vessel.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (OB, trauma positioning)
questions.q: A patient who is 34 weeks pregnant is secured to a long board after a crash. How should the board be positioned during transport?
options: Flat with the feet raised
Head down at 30 degrees
Upright at 90 degrees
Tilted toward her left side
questions.explain: Tilting the board to the left keeps the heavy uterus from pressing on the inferior vena cava, which could cause low blood pressure in the mother and reduced blood flow to the fetus. Raising the feet or lowering the head does not relieve this compression.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (OB, bleeding in late pregnancy)
questions.q: A woman at 32 weeks of pregnancy has heavy, painless, bright red vaginal bleeding and a rapid pulse. What is the priority?
options: Look inside the vagina for the source
Treat for shock and transport promptly
Pack the vagina to stop the bleeding
Have her walk to help the uterus settle
questions.explain: Heavy bleeding in late pregnancy can come from the placenta and lead to shock in the mother and harm to the fetus. The EMT places a pad over the vaginal opening, treats for shock and transports rapidly. Nothing is placed inside the vagina.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (cardiac arrest sequence)
questions.q: An adult is unresponsive, not breathing and has no pulse. In what order should care begin?
options: Airway, then breathing, then compressions
Breathing, then compressions, then airway
Airway, then compressions, then breathing
Compressions, then airway, then breathing
questions.explain: For adult cardiac arrest, the sequence is compressions, airway, breathing, because moving oxygenated blood quickly matters most and starting compressions avoids delays. For patients with a pulse, the airway and breathing are assessed and managed first.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (breathing assessment, hypoxia)
questions.q: Which is an early sign of hypoxia?
options: Blue lips and nail beds
A slowing heart rate
No response to pain
Restlessness and anxiety
questions.explain: The brain is sensitive to low oxygen, so restlessness, anxiety and confusion appear early, along with a fast heart rate. Cyanosis, a slowing heart rate and unresponsiveness are late signs that call for immediate airway and ventilation support.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (breathing assessment, pediatric work of breathing)
questions.q: A 2-year-old with difficulty breathing shows skin pulling in between the ribs with each breath. What does this indicate?
options: Normal breathing for a toddler
A rib fracture from a fall
Low blood sugar in the child
Increased work of breathing
questions.explain: Retractions between the ribs, above the collarbones or below the sternum show the child is working hard to breathe. Other signs include nasal flaring, grunting and head bobbing. These children need oxygen, a position of comfort and close monitoring for fatigue.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (breathing assessment, posture)
questions.q: A patient with COPD is sitting upright, leaning forward with the hands on the knees. What does this position suggest?
options: Abdominal pain only
Low blood sugar
Respiratory distress
A normal resting posture
questions.explain: This tripod position helps the patient use accessory muscles to move air, and it is a sign of significant respiratory distress. The patient is allowed to stay in this position of comfort and is not forced to lie flat.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway and ventilation, opioid overdose)
questions.q: A patient with a suspected opioid overdose is unresponsive, has a pulse and is breathing 4 times per minute. What is the first priority?
options: Open the airway and ventilate with a BVM
Give naloxone before any other care
Obtain a blood glucose reading
Search the area for drug items
questions.explain: Inadequate breathing is the immediate threat, so the airway is opened and ventilations are given with a BVM and oxygen. Naloxone is given as soon as practical, but it takes time to work and ventilation is not delayed for it.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (ventilation, stoma)
questions.q: A patient who breathes through a neck stoma needs ventilations. How should you deliver them?
options: Ventilate through the mouth and nose
Cover the stoma with a dry dressing first
Seal a small mask over the stoma and ventilate
Insert an oral airway into the stoma
questions.explain: A patient who has had the larynx removed breathes through the stoma, so ventilations go through it, often with an infant or child mask for a good seal. Covering the stoma blocks the airway. If air escapes from the mouth or nose, they may need to be sealed.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (ventilation, gastric distention)
questions.q: While you ventilate a patient with a BVM, the abdomen grows larger. What is the likely cause?
options: Breaths given too fast or with too much force
A mask sized slightly too small for the face
Oxygen flow to the bag set a little too low
Blood collecting in the patient's lungs
questions.explain: Air pushed in too quickly or with too much volume enters the esophagus and inflates the stomach, which can cause vomiting and limit lung expansion. Each breath is given over about 1 second, with just enough volume to see the chest rise, at the proper rate.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (ventilation, tidal volume)
questions.q: How much volume should each BVM ventilation deliver to an adult?
options: The full bag squeezed as hard as possible
A small puff that causes no chest rise
Enough to make the chest visibly rise
Twice the patient's usual breath size
questions.explain: The goal is visible chest rise with each breath, delivered over about 1 second. Squeezing hard or overfilling the lungs leads to stomach inflation and higher pressure in the chest, which lowers blood return to the heart.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (oxygenation, pulse oximetry limits)
questions.q: In which situation may a pulse oximeter show a falsely normal reading?
options: A patient with a normal pulse
A well-warmed finger
Carbon monoxide poisoning
A patient breathing room air
questions.explain: Standard pulse oximeters cannot tell oxygen from carbon monoxide bound to hemoglobin, so the reading may look normal while tissues are starved of oxygen. Cold fingers, poor perfusion and some nail polish can also cause inaccurate readings.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway protection, recovery position)
questions.q: An unresponsive adult with no suspected trauma is breathing adequately and has a pulse. How should the patient be positioned?
options: Flat on the back with the head still
In the recovery position on the side
Face down with the head turned
Sitting upright with the head forward
questions.explain: The recovery position keeps the airway open and lets fluids drain from the mouth, lowering the risk of aspiration. An unresponsive patient lying on the back can lose the airway to the tongue or vomit. Breathing is monitored continuously.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway, active seizure)
questions.q: A patient is having a generalized seizure. What should you do during the seizure?
options: Place a bite block between the teeth
Protect the patient from injury
Hold the arms and legs to stop jerking
Pour water in the mouth to wake them
questions.explain: During a seizure, the EMT moves objects away, cushions the head and does not restrain movement or put anything in the mouth. After the seizure, the airway is opened and suctioned as needed and oxygen is given. A long or repeated seizure needs urgent care.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (newborn resuscitation, ventilation)
questions.q: A newborn is not breathing after being dried, warmed and stimulated. What should you do?
options: Start chest compressions right away
Keep stimulating for two more minutes
Hold the newborn upside down
Begin ventilations with a BVM
questions.explain: Most newborns who need help respond to effective ventilation. If a newborn is apneic or gasping, or has a heart rate below 100 per minute after the initial steps, ventilation with a BVM begins at 40 to 60 breaths per minute.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (newborn resuscitation, compressions)
questions.q: A newborn's heart rate stays below 60 per minute despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation. What should be added?
options: Chest compressions at a 3 to 1 ratio
Oral glucose placed in the cheek
Chest compressions at a 30 to 2 ratio
Back slaps given between breaths
questions.explain: In newborn resuscitation, a heart rate below 60 per minute despite effective ventilation calls for chest compressions coordinated with breaths at 3 compressions to 1 breath. The 30 to 2 ratio is for single-rescuer CPR in older patients.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (priority decisions, multiple patients)
questions.q: You have two patients: one with a broken arm who is screaming in pain, and one who is quiet with snoring respirations. Whom do you treat first?
options: The screaming patient with the broken arm
Both equally, switching every minute
The quiet patient with snoring respirations
Whoever was injured first at the scene
questions.explain: Snoring respirations in a quiet patient suggest decreased responsiveness and a partly blocked airway, an immediate life threat. A patient who can scream has an open airway and is breathing. Airway problems are managed before painful but stable injuries.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (circulation and breathing, anaphylaxis recognition)
questions.q: A patient stung by a bee has hives, wheezing and a weak, rapid pulse. What do these findings suggest?
options: A local reaction needing ice
Anxiety needing reassurance
Mild asthma needing rest only
Anaphylaxis needing epinephrine
questions.explain: Hives together with breathing difficulty and signs of shock indicate anaphylaxis, a life-threatening allergic reaction. Epinephrine by auto-injector is the key treatment, followed by rapid transport. A local reaction involves only swelling at the sting site.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (breathing assessment, pediatric respiratory failure)
questions.q: A 4-year-old with asthma was struggling to breathe but now seems sleepy, with slower and weaker breaths. What does this suggest?
options: The asthma attack is ending normally
The child is calm because care worked
The child is tiring and may be near failure
The child simply needs to take a nap
questions.explain: A child who goes from working hard to breathe to drowsy with slow, shallow breathing is likely exhausted and in respiratory failure. This calls for assisted ventilation with a BVM and immediate transport. Real improvement looks like easier breathing with good alertness.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (pediatric assessment triangle)
questions.q: Which three components make up the Pediatric Assessment Triangle?
options: Airway, blood pressure, pupil response
Appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin
Pulse, temperature, blood glucose level
Speech, arm drift, facial symmetry
questions.explain: The Pediatric Assessment Triangle is a quick look from across the room at the child's appearance, work of breathing and circulation to the skin. It helps the EMT judge how sick a child is before touching the child. Speech, arm drift and facial symmetry belong to a stroke scale.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (oxygen devices, pediatric blow-by)
questions.q: A frightened 3-year-old with breathing difficulty will not tolerate a mask. How can you give oxygen?
options: Hold the mask or tubing near the child's face
Strap the mask on firmly while the child cries
Withhold oxygen until hospital arrival
Give oxygen only by bag-valve mask
questions.explain: Blow-by oxygen, with the mask or tubing held near the face, often by a parent, delivers some oxygen without upsetting the child. Forcing a mask on increases crying and oxygen demand and can worsen airway swelling. A BVM is for inadequate breathing.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Primary Assessment (airway, pediatric upper airway infection)
questions.q: A child has stridor and drooling and sits leaning forward, refusing to lie down. What should you avoid?
options: Looking in the throat with a tongue depressor
Letting a parent hold the child
Keeping the child in a position of comfort
Giving blow-by oxygen near the face
questions.explain: These signs suggest a serious upper airway infection, and probing the throat can trigger spasm and complete obstruction. The EMT keeps the child calm in a position of comfort, gives oxygen as tolerated and transports promptly.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Secondary Assessment (SAMPLE history)
questions.q: In a SAMPLE history, what does the letter E stand for?
options: Exposure to heat or cold
Examination of the extremities
Events leading up to the illness or injury
Estimated time of arrival
questions.explain: SAMPLE stands for Signs and symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Pertinent past history, Last oral intake and Events leading to the problem. Asking what the patient was doing when symptoms began helps identify the cause.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Secondary Assessment (OPQRST)
questions.q: When assessing chest pain with OPQRST, which question addresses provocation?
options: When did the pain first start?
Does the pain spread anywhere?
How bad is it on a scale of 1 to 10?
Does anything make the pain better or worse?
questions.explain: Provocation, or palliation, asks what makes the pain better or worse, such as movement, breathing or rest. Onset is when it started, radiation is where it spreads, and severity is the 1 to 10 rating.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Secondary Assessment (vital signs, infant heart rate)
questions.q: Which resting heart rate in an infant is too slow and needs immediate attention?
options: 120 beats per minute
130 beats per minute
140 beats per minute
70 beats per minute
questions.explain: A resting infant's heart rate is normally well above 100 beats per minute. A rate of 70 is too slow, and in infants a slow heart rate is often caused by hypoxia, so oxygenation and ventilation are checked right away. The other rates fall in the expected range.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Secondary Assessment (vital signs, blood pressure by palpation)
questions.q: When taking a blood pressure by palpation, what can you measure?
options: Diastolic pressure only
Systolic pressure only
Both systolic and diastolic
Mean arterial pressure only
questions.explain: By palpation, the EMT feels for the radial pulse returning as the cuff deflates, which gives the systolic pressure. The diastolic pressure requires listening with a stethoscope. Palpation is useful in noisy settings.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Secondary Assessment (blood glucose)
questions.q: A patient with diabetes is confused and sweaty. Which blood glucose reading supports hypoglycemia?
options: 52 mg/dL
95 mg/dL
110 mg/dL
140 mg/dL
questions.explain: A blood glucose below about 70 mg/dL is generally considered low, and confusion, sweating and shakiness are common symptoms. A reading of 52 mg/dL with these signs supports giving glucose if the patient can swallow. The other readings are in or near the normal range.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Secondary Assessment (stroke scales)
questions.q: Which test is part of the Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale?
options: A fingerstick blood glucose
Pupil reaction to a light
Walking heel to toe in a line
Arm drift with the eyes closed
questions.explain: The Cincinnati scale checks for facial droop when smiling, arm drift when both arms are held out with the eyes closed, and abnormal speech. One abnormal finding raises concern for stroke. Blood glucose is also checked because low sugar can mimic stroke, but it is not part of the scale.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Secondary Assessment (stroke, time last known well)
questions.q: Why is it important to find out when a stroke patient was last known well?
options: It decides which ambulance should respond
It sets the oxygen flow rate to be used
It tells the hospital the patient's age
It guides which treatments may be possible
questions.explain: Many stroke treatments must start within limited time windows, so the time the patient was last seen normal guides hospital decisions and the choice of destination. If the patient woke up with symptoms, the last known well time is when he or she went to sleep.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Secondary Assessment (trauma exam, DCAP-BTLS)
questions.q: During a trauma exam, what does the letter B stand for in DCAP-BTLS?
options: Burns
Bleeding
Bruising
Breathing
questions.explain: DCAP-BTLS lists findings to look and feel for: Deformities, Contusions, Abrasions, Punctures or penetrations, Burns, Tenderness, Lacerations and Swelling. Bruising is covered by contusions, and bleeding is managed in the primary assessment.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Secondary Assessment (neurological exam, pupils)
questions.q: After a head injury, one pupil is dilated and does not react to light. What does this suggest?
options: A normal reaction to bright light
Low blood sugar and nothing else
Simple irritation of the eye
Rising pressure inside the skull
questions.explain: A single dilated, nonreactive pupil after head trauma can mean pressure on the nerve from bleeding or swelling inside the skull. It is a serious finding that calls for rapid transport and frequent reassessment of mental status and vital signs.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Secondary Assessment (full-body exam, significant mechanism)
questions.q: A patient was ejected from a vehicle and responds only to pain. Which assessment should follow the primary assessment?
options: A focused exam of a single complaint
A detailed exam before any treatment
A SAMPLE history from the patient
A rapid full-body trauma assessment
questions.explain: A significant mechanism and altered mental status call for a rapid head-to-toe exam to find hidden life threats. A focused exam suits isolated injuries with a minor mechanism. This patient cannot give a reliable history, so information comes from bystanders.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Secondary Assessment (focused exam, chest trauma)
questions.q: A patient with chest trauma has distended neck veins while sitting upright. What might this indicate?
options: A normal finding after exertion
Dehydration from blood loss
Increased pressure within the chest
A low blood sugar level
questions.explain: Jugular vein distention in a sitting patient suggests blood is backing up because of increased pressure in the chest, as with tension pneumothorax or pericardial tamponade, or from heart failure. Blood loss usually causes flat neck veins.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Secondary Assessment (focused exam, medical patient)
questions.q: A responsive patient complains only of abdominal pain. Which secondary assessment approach fits?
options: A rapid full-body trauma survey
A focused exam of the abdomen and related areas
No exam until arrival at the hospital
An exam of the arms and legs only
questions.explain: For a responsive medical patient with one complaint, the history guides a focused exam of the affected area, such as inspecting and gently palpating the abdomen. A rapid full-body exam is for unresponsive or seriously injured patients.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, oral glucose)
questions.q: Which patient is appropriate to receive oral glucose?
options: An unresponsive diabetic with low blood sugar
An alert diabetic who can swallow and feels shaky
A patient having a seizure with known diabetes
A patient with a very high blood sugar reading
questions.explain: Oral glucose is given to patients with suspected low blood sugar who are awake enough to swallow and protect their airway. Unresponsive or seizing patients could choke or aspirate. Giving sugar to a patient with high blood glucose does not treat the problem.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, aspirin contraindications)
questions.q: A patient with chest pain suspected to be cardiac might receive aspirin. Which finding is a reason not to give it?
options: Pain that began 20 minutes ago
A known allergy to aspirin
A history of high blood pressure
An age of more than 50 years
questions.explain: Aspirin reduces clot formation in acute coronary syndrome, but it is not given to patients who are allergic to it or, per protocol, who have recent gastrointestinal bleeding. Age and high blood pressure are common in cardiac patients and do not prevent aspirin use.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, aspirin administration)
questions.q: How is aspirin given for suspected acute coronary syndrome at the EMT level?
options: Swallowed whole with water
Dissolved under the tongue
Chewed, using low-dose tablets
Injected into a muscle
questions.explain: Chewing aspirin speeds absorption so its antiplatelet effect begins sooner. Low-dose chewable tablets totaling about 160 to 325 mg are typical, as protocol directs. Placing a tablet under the tongue is the route for nitroglycerin.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, nitroglycerin contraindications)
questions.q: A patient with chest pain has his own prescribed nitroglycerin. He took a medication for erectile dysfunction yesterday. What should you do?
options: Not assist with nitroglycerin and inform medical control
Assist with one tablet only and then reassess
Assist with half of the usual tablet dose
Assist only if the pain is above 5 of 10
questions.explain: Erectile dysfunction drugs combined with nitroglycerin can cause a severe drop in blood pressure. Nitroglycerin is withheld when such drugs were taken recently, usually within 24 to 48 hours depending on the drug. A smaller dose does not remove the risk.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, assisting with nitroglycerin)
questions.q: Before assisting a patient with nitroglycerin, which condition must be met?
options: The medication is prescribed to that patient
The patient has never had chest pain before
The patient has eaten within the last hour
The patient has already taken an aspirin
questions.explain: EMTs assist only with nitroglycerin prescribed to the patient, after confirming the right drug, an adequate blood pressure per protocol and medical direction approval. A first episode of chest pain, recent eating or prior aspirin do not determine eligibility.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, nitroglycerin side effects)
questions.q: After taking nitroglycerin, a patient reports a throbbing headache. What explains this?
options: Widening of blood vessels by the drug
An allergic reaction to the tablet
A stroke caused by the medication
A rise in blood sugar from the drug
questions.explain: Nitroglycerin relaxes and widens blood vessels, which commonly causes headache, flushing and a drop in blood pressure. Blood pressure is rechecked after each dose. A headache alone is an expected side effect, not an allergy.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, metered-dose inhaler)
questions.q: When assisting a patient with a prescribed metered-dose inhaler, what should the patient do?
options: Inhale fully, then press it while breathing out
Press it twice quickly without breathing in
Hold it away from the mouth and then press it
Exhale fully, then inhale deeply as it is pressed
questions.explain: The patient shakes the inhaler, exhales fully, seals the lips around the mouthpiece or spacer, presses the inhaler while breathing in slowly and deeply, then holds the breath as long as comfortable. This carries the medication into the lungs.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, epinephrine auto-injector site)
questions.q: Where is an epinephrine auto-injector given?
options: The outer thigh
The upper arm
The buttock
The abdomen
questions.explain: Epinephrine auto-injectors are given into the lateral thigh muscle, which absorbs the drug quickly and can be reached through clothing if needed. The device is held in place for the time the manufacturer specifies, and the used injector is disposed of safely.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, epinephrine dose)
questions.q: What is the standard adult epinephrine auto-injector dose?
options: 1 mg
3 mg
0.3 mg
questions.explain: The adult auto-injector delivers 0.3 mg of epinephrine into the thigh muscle, while the pediatric version delivers 0.15 mg for smaller children. Larger doses are not given by auto-injector and could cause dangerous heart effects.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, epinephrine action)
questions.q: Why is epinephrine given in anaphylaxis?
options: It slows the heart and lowers blood pressure
It blocks pain signals from the sting site
It narrows blood vessels and opens the airways
It raises blood sugar to prevent fainting
questions.explain: Epinephrine constricts blood vessels to raise blood pressure and relaxes airway muscle to ease breathing, reversing key effects of anaphylaxis. It speeds the heart rate, so side effects include palpitations, anxiety and tremors.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, naloxone)
questions.q: Which patient is most appropriate for intranasal naloxone given by an EMT?
options: Unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and slow breathing
Alert with chest pain after exercising
Confused with a low blood glucose reading
Agitated with fast breathing and a fever
questions.explain: Naloxone reverses opioid effects and is indicated for suspected opioid overdose with depressed breathing. Pinpoint pupils, unresponsiveness and slow breathing are classic signs. Ventilation is supported while naloxone takes effect, and the patient may wake agitated or in withdrawal.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, oxygen in COPD)
questions.q: A patient with COPD is in severe respiratory distress with an oxygen saturation of 82 percent. What is appropriate?
options: Withhold oxygen because of the COPD
Give oxygen only after hospital arrival
Give oxygen and monitor breathing closely
Limit oxygen to 0.5 liters per minute
questions.explain: Hypoxia must be corrected in any patient in distress. Patients with COPD receive oxygen titrated to the target saturation in the protocol while the EMT watches their breathing and mental status. Withholding oxygen from a hypoxic patient is dangerous.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (respiratory support, CPAP)
questions.q: Which patient is appropriate for continuous positive airway pressure?
options: An unresponsive patient without a gag reflex
An alert patient with fluid in the lungs who breathes on his own
A patient with a suspected collapsed lung
A patient with low blood pressure who is vomiting
questions.explain: CPAP helps alert, cooperative patients in respiratory distress from causes such as pulmonary edema, who are still breathing on their own. It is contraindicated when the patient cannot protect the airway, has low blood pressure, is vomiting or may have a pneumothorax.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (splinting, long bones)
questions.q: When splinting a suspected forearm fracture, what should the splint immobilize?
options: The wrist and the elbow
The forearm alone
The shoulder and elbow
The fingers alone
questions.explain: A long-bone fracture is splinted so the joints above and below the injury, here the elbow and wrist, are immobilized. This prevents movement of the bone ends that causes pain and further damage. The hand is placed in the position of function.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (splinting, distal checks)
questions.q: When should you check pulse, motor function and sensation in an injured extremity?
options: Before and after applying the splint
Only before applying the splint
Only once at the hospital
Only after the splint is on
questions.explain: Checking distal circulation, movement and sensation before and after splinting shows whether the injury or the splint is affecting nerves or blood flow. A loss after splinting means the splint may be too tight and needs adjusting.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (splinting, joint injuries)
questions.q: A patient has a deformed knee injury with a good distal pulse. How should you splint it?
options: In the position found
Fully straightened first
Bent to 90 degrees first
With a traction splint
questions.explain: Joint injuries are splinted in the position found when circulation is intact, because moving them can damage nerves and vessels. Traction splints are contraindicated for knee injuries. Protocols address what to do if the distal pulse is absent.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (splinting, traction splint)
questions.q: Which injury is an indication for a traction splint?
options: A fracture next to the ankle joint
An isolated midshaft femur fracture
A suspected fracture of the pelvis
A dislocation of the knee joint
questions.explain: Traction splints reduce pain and bleeding from isolated, closed midshaft femur fractures by keeping the bone aligned. They are not used for pelvis, hip, knee or ankle injuries, because traction would pull across those injured areas.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (splinting, pelvic binder)
questions.q: Where should a pelvic binder be placed?
options: Around the waist at the belly button
Around the hips at the greater trochanters
Around the lower ribs below the chest
Around the upper thighs below the hips
questions.explain: A pelvic binder is centered over the greater trochanters, the bony points at the sides of the hips, to stabilize an unstable pelvic fracture and limit bleeding. Placing it at the waist does not compress the pelvic ring.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (spinal motion restriction, indications)
questions.q: After a fall, which patient most clearly meets criteria for spinal motion restriction?
options: An alert patient with only a wrist injury
A patient with midline neck pain and tingling arms
A patient walking around with a bruised knee
An alert patient with a small cut on the scalp
questions.explain: Spinal motion restriction is indicated for patients with midline spine pain or tenderness, neurological deficits, altered mental status or intoxication, or distracting injuries after a concerning mechanism. Tingling in the arms with neck pain suggests possible spinal cord injury.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (spinal motion restriction, manual stabilization)
questions.q: When can manual stabilization of the head be released?
options: As soon as a cervical collar is in place
When the patient is fully secured to a device
Once the patient says the neck feels fine
After the first set of vital signs
questions.explain: A cervical collar alone does not fully prevent movement, so manual stabilization continues until the patient is secured to a device, such as a long board, scoop or vacuum mattress, with the head immobilized. The patient's own report is not reliable for this.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (burns, rule of nines)
questions.q: Using the rule of nines, what percentage of body surface area is one entire arm in an adult?
options: 18 percent
4.5 percent
9 percent
1 percent
questions.explain: In the adult rule of nines, each arm is 9 percent, each leg 18 percent, the front and the back of the trunk 18 percent each, the head 9 percent and the genital area 1 percent. The patient's palm is about 1 percent and can be used to estimate scattered burns.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (burns, pediatric body surface area)
questions.q: Compared with an adult, which body area makes up a larger share of total body surface area in an infant?
options: Each leg
Each arm
The genitals
The head
