questions.explain: Infants have relatively large heads, which make up about 18 percent of body surface area in the pediatric rule of nines, compared with 9 percent in adults. Each leg makes up a smaller share. Burn size in infants is estimated with the pediatric chart.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (burns, thermal burn care)
questions.q: After the burning process is stopped on a small thermal burn, what should you do?
options: Apply ice directly onto the burned area
Spread butter or a greasy ointment on it
Break the blisters so the fluid drains
Cool it briefly with clean water, then cover it dry
questions.explain: Cooling a small burn with water stops further damage, and a dry sterile dressing protects it. Ice injures tissue, and greasy substances trap heat and complicate hospital care. Blisters are left intact to protect against infection. Large burns are not cooled for long because of hypothermia risk.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (burns, dry chemicals)
questions.q: A worker has a dry chemical powder on both arms. What should you do first?
options: Flush with a little water right away
Rub the powder off with a damp cloth
Brush off the powder, then flush with water
Cover the powder with a dry dressing
questions.explain: Some dry chemicals react with water, so as much powder as possible is brushed off before flushing with large amounts of water. Contaminated clothing is removed. EMTs protect themselves from contact while doing this.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (burns, electrical injuries)
questions.q: A patient touched a high-voltage line and has small burns on one hand and one foot. What is the main concern?
options: Infection of the small skin wounds
Scarring of the hand over time
Internal damage and heart rhythm problems
Dehydration from heavy sweating
questions.explain: Electric current travels through the body, damaging deep tissues and possibly causing dangerous heart rhythms, even when skin burns look small. The entry and exit wounds suggest the path of the current. The patient is monitored closely with the AED kept ready.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (childbirth, imminent delivery)
questions.q: During labor, the baby's head is visible at the vaginal opening with each contraction. What should you do?
options: Prepare to deliver on scene
Transport with lights and siren
Have the mother cross her legs
Ask the mother to hold back
questions.explain: Crowning means delivery is near, so the EMT prepares to deliver on scene rather than risk a birth in a moving ambulance. The mother is never asked to hold back the delivery. Gentle support of the head helps prevent an explosive birth.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (childbirth, nuchal cord)
questions.q: As the head delivers, you feel the umbilical cord wrapped loosely around the baby's neck. What should you do?
options: Pull the baby out quickly by the head
Gently slip the cord over the baby's head
Push the baby back into the vagina
Wait for the next contraction to check
questions.explain: A loose cord around the neck is slipped over the head or shoulders so delivery can continue. If it is too tight to slip, protocols call for clamping it in two places and cutting between the clamps. Pulling on the baby can injure it.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (newborn care, initial steps)
questions.q: Right after delivery, the newborn is crying and has good muscle tone. What should you do next?
options: Hold the newborn upside down by the feet
Cut the cord within the first few seconds
Start ventilations with a BVM right away
Dry and warm the newborn
questions.explain: Drying and warming prevent heat loss, which newborns suffer quickly. A crying newborn with good tone usually needs only routine care and can be placed skin to skin with the mother. Holding a newborn by the feet is unsafe, and cord clamping is commonly delayed in vigorous newborns.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (childbirth, limb presentation)
questions.q: During labor, an arm is the first part of the baby to come out of the vagina. What should you do?
options: Position the mother and transport rapidly
Pull gently on the arm to deliver
Push the arm back into the vagina
Stay on scene and wait for delivery
questions.explain: A limb presentation cannot be delivered in the field and requires surgery. The EMT covers the limb, positions the mother to reduce pressure, gives oxygen as needed and transports immediately. Pulling or pushing on the limb can injure the baby and the mother.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (childbirth, prolapsed cord)
questions.q: The umbilical cord comes out before the baby during labor. What should you do?
options: Push the cord back up inside the vagina
Keep the presenting part off the cord with gloved fingers
Clamp and cut the cord right away
Have the mother push hard to speed birth
questions.explain: A prolapsed cord can be squeezed by the baby's head, cutting off oxygen. The EMT places the mother in a knee-chest or hips-raised position, uses gloved fingers to keep pressure off the cord and transports rapidly. The cord is kept moist and is not pushed back.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (childbirth, postpartum bleeding)
questions.q: After the placenta delivers, the mother is bleeding heavily. What can you do to help the uterus contract?
options: Massage the top of the uterus
Pack gauze inside the vagina
Lay her flat with legs crossed
Give her water to drink often
questions.explain: Firm massage of the top of the uterus, the fundus, helps it contract and close bleeding vessels. Breastfeeding also helps the uterus contract. Nothing is placed inside the vagina, and the mother is treated for shock and transported.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (newborn care, APGAR)
questions.q: Which items are scored in the APGAR assessment of a newborn?
options: Airway, pressure, glucose, alertness, rhythm
Age, pupils, gestation, arms, reflexes
Appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, respirations
Allergies, pain, gait, attention, reach
questions.explain: APGAR scores appearance or skin color, pulse, grimace or reflex response, activity or muscle tone, and respirations, each from 0 to 2, at 1 and 5 minutes after birth. Resuscitation is never delayed to obtain the score.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (environmental emergencies, heat stroke)
questions.q: A runner on a hot day is confused and has hot skin. What is the priority?
options: Oral fluids and rest in the shade only
Warm blankets to prevent shivering
Salt tablets with a sports drink
Rapid cooling and prompt transport
questions.explain: Altered mental status with a high body temperature indicates heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency. Aggressive cooling starts at once, such as removing clothing, applying cold packs to the neck, armpits and groin, and wetting and fanning the skin. Oral fluids are unsafe in a confused patient.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (environmental emergencies, hypothermia)
questions.q: Why should a patient with severe hypothermia be handled gently?
options: Rough handling can warm the patient too quickly
Rough handling can trigger dangerous heart rhythms
Cold skin tears more easily than warm skin
Movement makes the patient start to shiver
questions.explain: A very cold heart is irritable, and jostling can provoke ventricular fibrillation. The EMT moves the patient gently, removes wet clothing, insulates the patient and begins passive warming. Pulse checks may take longer because the pulse can be slow and weak.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (environmental emergencies, frostbite)
questions.q: A patient has frostbite of the toes, and transport to the hospital will be short. What should you do?
options: Rub the toes briskly with clean snow
Have the patient walk to warm them up
Protect the area and avoid rubbing it
Rewarm them close to a heater flame
questions.explain: Rubbing frozen tissue causes more damage, and walking on frozen feet injures them further. Direct heat can burn numb skin. The area is protected with dry dressings, and rewarming is usually left to the hospital, especially if refreezing could occur.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (environmental emergencies, drowning)
questions.q: A swimmer pulled from the water is unresponsive and not breathing but has a pulse. What is the priority?
options: Give abdominal thrusts to drain water
Begin rescue breaths with a BVM
Wait for the patient to cough it up
Warm the patient before any breaths
questions.explain: Drowning causes hypoxia, so restoring oxygen with ventilation is the priority. Abdominal thrusts to remove water are not recommended because they delay ventilation and risk vomiting. The patient is also protected from cold and transported.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (environmental emergencies, snakebite)
questions.q: A hiker was bitten on the lower leg by a venomous snake. What is appropriate care?
options: Apply ice packs over the bite site
Cut the bite and suck out the venom
Keep the patient calm and the limb still
Apply a tight tourniquet above it
questions.explain: Keeping the patient calm and the limb immobilized slows the spread of venom. Jewelry and tight clothing are removed before swelling starts. Ice, cutting, suction and tourniquets cause more tissue damage and are not recommended. Transport to a facility with antivenom is key.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (transport positioning, heart failure)
questions.q: A patient with heart failure is short of breath with crackles in both lungs. How should you transport the patient?
options: Sitting upright
Flat on the back
Head lower than the feet
Face down on the stretcher
questions.explain: Sitting upright lets fluid settle in the lower lungs and makes breathing easier. Lying flat worsens shortness of breath in heart failure. The patient's position of comfort is usually upright.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (reassessment intervals)
questions.q: How often should you reassess vital signs in an unstable patient?
options: About every 5 minutes
About every 15 minutes
About every 30 minutes
Only once during transport
questions.explain: Unstable patients can change quickly, so vital signs and the primary assessment are repeated about every 5 minutes. Stable patients are reassessed about every 15 minutes. Any change in condition calls for immediate reassessment.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (medications, oral glucose in a child)
questions.q: A 7-year-old with diabetes is unresponsive with a blood glucose of 38 mg/dL. Why should you not give oral glucose?
options: Oral glucose is never used in children
The child cannot protect the airway
The level is not low enough to treat
Oral glucose raises sugar too quickly
questions.explain: Oral glucose requires a patient who can swallow and protect the airway, and an unresponsive child could aspirate it. The EMT manages the airway, requests advanced life support if available and transports promptly. Oral glucose can be used in children who are awake and able to swallow.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (eye injuries, chemical exposure)
questions.q: A patient splashed a cleaning chemical into both eyes. What should you do?
options: Patch both eyes closed and transport
Rinse once quickly and then cover
Flush the eyes with water for a long time
Rub the eyes to remove the chemical
questions.explain: Chemical eye injuries need immediate, continuous flushing with large amounts of clean water or saline, typically for at least 15 to 20 minutes and continued during transport. The water flows from the inner corner outward so it does not run into the other eye.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (soft tissue injuries, impaled object)
questions.q: A patient has a metal rod impaled in the thigh. What should you do?
options: Remove it and then apply direct pressure
Cut it flush with the surface of the skin
Twist it slightly to check how deep it is
Stabilize the object in place with bulky dressings
questions.explain: Removing an impaled object can cause severe bleeding and more damage, so it is stabilized in place with bulky dressings. Exceptions include an object in the cheek that blocks the airway, or one that prevents CPR. Bleeding around the object is controlled with pressure.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (soft tissue injuries, evisceration)
questions.q: A patient has abdominal organs protruding from a wound. How should you care for it?
options: Cover with a moist sterile dressing, then an occlusive one
Push the organs gently back inside the abdomen
Cover with dry gauze and press down firmly
Rinse the organs with cold tap water first
questions.explain: Eviscerated organs are covered with sterile dressings moistened with sterile saline, then with an occlusive layer to keep in moisture and heat. They are never pushed back in. Dry dressings stick to the organs and damage them.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (soft tissue injuries, amputation)
questions.q: How should an amputated finger be prepared for transport?
options: Placed directly in a cup of ice water
Wrapped in dry towels at room temperature
Wrapped in moist gauze, bagged and kept cool
Packed directly on dry ice to freeze it
questions.explain: The part is wrapped in sterile gauze moistened as protocol directs, sealed in a plastic bag and kept cool without direct contact with ice, which can freeze and destroy tissue. It is transported with the patient.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Patient Treatment and Transport (bleeding, nosebleed)
questions.q: A patient has a nosebleed without any trauma. How should the patient be positioned?
options: Sitting up, leaning forward, pinching the nostrils
Lying flat with the head tilted back
Sitting up with the head tilted back
Lying on the side with no pressure
questions.explain: Leaning forward keeps blood from running down the throat, where it can be swallowed or aspirated and cause vomiting. Firmly pinching the soft part of the nose applies direct pressure. Tilting the head back hides ongoing bleeding.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (consent, implied)
questions.q: An unresponsive adult is found after a fall. Under which type of consent do you provide care?
options: Expressed consent
Informed refusal
Implied consent
Involuntary consent
questions.explain: Implied consent assumes that a reasonable person who cannot respond would want lifesaving care. Expressed consent comes from a competent, alert adult who agrees to care. If the patient regains consciousness and is competent, he or she may then accept or refuse care.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (consent, minors)
questions.q: A 10-year-old is seriously injured at school, and a parent cannot be reached right away. What should you do?
options: Wait until a parent gives consent before treating
Have the child sign a consent form before treating
Refuse to treat until a guardian arrives on scene
Treat under implied consent and keep trying to reach a parent
questions.explain: Minors generally cannot give legal consent, so consent comes from a parent or guardian. In an emergency when they cannot be reached, care is given under implied consent. Delaying treatment of a serious injury to obtain permission is not appropriate.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (refusal of care)
questions.q: A competent adult with chest pain refuses transport. What should you do?
options: Explain the risks and document the refusal
Transport the patient against his will
Leave right away without documenting
Have a family member sign for him
questions.explain: A competent adult may refuse care after being informed of the risks, including death. The EMT tries to persuade, explains the risks, advises calling back, involves medical control per protocol and documents the refusal with signatures. Transporting a competent adult against his will can be battery.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (abandonment)
questions.q: Which action by an EMT is an example of abandonment?
options: Turning care over to a paramedic crew
Leaving a patient before care is transferred
Honoring a competent patient's refusal
Handing off care with a verbal report
questions.explain: Abandonment is ending care once it has begun without making sure the patient is turned over to someone with equal or higher training. Transferring care to a paramedic or hospital staff with a report is appropriate.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (HIPAA)
questions.q: Which disclosure of patient information is permitted under HIPAA?
options: Giving a report to the receiving hospital
Telling a neighbor about the illness
Posting call details on social media
Discussing the patient with friends
questions.explain: HIPAA allows protected health information to be shared for treatment, payment and health care operations, so reporting to the receiving hospital is permitted. Sharing details with neighbors, friends or online audiences violates patient privacy.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (mandatory reporting, child abuse)
questions.q: A 4-year-old has bruises in different stages of healing, and the parent's story does not match the injuries. What should you do?
options: Treat the child and report as required by law
Confront the parent about the abuse
Leave without treating to avoid conflict
Ignore it since there is no proof
questions.explain: EMTs are mandated reporters of suspected child abuse in most states. Proof is not required, only reasonable suspicion. The EMT provides care, documents objective findings and reports to the proper authority without accusing the parent.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (documentation, correcting errors)
questions.q: You made a mistake in a written patient care report. How should you correct it?
options: Erase it completely and rewrite it
Cover it with correction fluid
Tear out the page and start over
Draw one line through it, then initial and date it
questions.explain: A single line through the error keeps it readable and shows an honest correction, with initials and the date. Erasing or covering errors can suggest falsification. Electronic reports have their own amendment process.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (documentation, falsification)
questions.q: An EMT forgot to give oxygen but writes in the report that it was given. What is this?
options: An acceptable charting shortcut
A minor timing error
Falsification of the report
A permitted report summary
questions.explain: Recording care that was not given is falsification, which can lead to legal action and loss of certification and can mislead the next caregivers. Omissions are documented honestly, along with what was actually done.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (ambulance operations, emergency driving)
questions.q: When driving with lights and siren, what must the ambulance operator do?
options: Drive with due regard for the safety of others
Pass through red lights at full speed
Assume other drivers will always yield
Disregard all posted speed limits
questions.explain: Emergency vehicle laws allow certain exemptions, but the driver must still use due regard for the safety of others. Other drivers may not hear or see the ambulance, so the operator slows and stops as needed at intersections.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (lifting and moving, body mechanics)
questions.q: Which technique helps an EMT lift a stretcher safely?
options: Bend at the waist and lift with the back
Twist while lifting to save a step
Keep the feet together while lifting
Keep the back straight and lift with the legs
questions.explain: The power lift uses a straight back, feet about shoulder width apart and the strong leg muscles to raise the load, keeping it close to the body. Bending at the waist or twisting puts heavy stress on the spine and causes injury.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (lifting and moving, emergency moves)
questions.q: A patient is in a car that is on fire. Which move is appropriate?
options: Full spinal immobilization before any movement
A standard stretcher transfer once fire is out
An emergency drag along the long axis of the body
Waiting for extrication tools to arrive first
questions.explain: When there is immediate danger, such as fire, the patient is moved quickly with an emergency move, pulling along the long axis of the body to limit spinal movement. Spinal precautions do not delay removal from a life-threatening hazard.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (lifting and moving, devices)
questions.q: A conscious patient with shortness of breath must be carried down a narrow staircase. Which device is best?
options: A stair chair
A long backboard
A scoop stretcher
A basket stretcher
questions.explain: A stair chair lets an alert patient sit upright, which eases breathing, and it is easy to carry on stairs. Lying a short-of-breath patient flat on a board or scoop worsens distress. Stair chairs are not used for unresponsive patients or suspected spinal injuries.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (incident command, first arriving unit)
questions.q: At a mass casualty incident, what should the first arriving EMS unit do?
options: Begin treating the closest patient
Establish command and size up the scene
Transport the most injured patient
Wait for a supervisor to arrive
questions.explain: The first arriving unit establishes command, assesses the scene, requests resources and begins organizing triage. Treating or transporting the first patient seen delays the system that will help everyone.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (incident command, MCI roles)
questions.q: Under the incident command system at a mass casualty incident, which role oversees sorting patients by priority?
options: The transport officer
The staging officer
The public information officer
The triage officer
questions.explain: The triage officer oversees rapid sorting and tagging of patients. The treatment officer manages care areas, the transport officer coordinates moving patients to hospitals, and the staging officer manages arriving units. The public information officer speaks with the media.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (communication, medical direction orders)
questions.q: Medical control gives an order by radio to assist with a medication. What should the EMT do?
options: Carry it out without replying
Ask the patient to approve it
Repeat the order back to confirm it
Write it down later from memory
questions.explain: Repeating the order word for word, called echoing, confirms the drug, dose and route and catches errors. If an order seems unclear or inappropriate, the EMT asks for clarification before acting.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (communication, radio report)
questions.q: Which information belongs in a radio report to the receiving hospital?
options: Full home address and phone number
Chief complaint, vital signs and care given
Insurance details and billing codes
The EMT's opinion of the family
questions.explain: A radio report is brief and gives the hospital what it needs to prepare: unit and level, age and sex, chief complaint, key findings, vital signs, care given, response to care and arrival time. Identifying details are limited on the radio for privacy.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (advance directives)
questions.q: A patient in cardiac arrest at home has a valid, signed do not resuscitate order that meets local requirements. What should you do?
options: Start CPR until the family agrees to stop
Ignore the order because it is not yours
Begin CPR and then call the physician
Honor the order and withhold resuscitation
questions.explain: A valid do not resuscitate or out-of-hospital order that meets state and local requirements reflects the patient's wishes and is honored. The EMT confirms validity, supports the family and documents. If validity is in doubt, resuscitation is generally started per protocol.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (legal concepts, negligence)
questions.q: To prove negligence against an EMT, what must be shown in addition to duty, breach of duty and damages?
options: Intent to harm the patient
A written patient complaint
A statement from a witness
Causation linking the breach to the harm
questions.explain: Negligence requires a duty to act, a breach of that duty, harm or damages, and causation showing that the breach caused the harm. Intent is not required for negligence. A complaint or a witness may be evidence but is not one of the elements.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (infection control, equipment cleaning)
questions.q: After transporting a patient, the crew finds blood on the stretcher. What should they do?
options: Clean and disinfect it per protocol
Wipe it with plain water only
Cover it with a clean sheet
Wait until end of shift to clean it
questions.explain: Blood on equipment can transmit infection, so it is cleaned and disinfected with an approved product before the next patient. Covering contamination with a sheet does not remove the risk. Crews wear gloves while cleaning.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (infection control, exposure response)
questions.q: An EMT is stuck by a used needle during a call. What should the EMT do first?
options: Finish the shift, then report it
Wash the site with soap and water
Wait to see if symptoms develop
Pour bleach into the puncture
questions.explain: After a needlestick, the site is washed with soap and water right away, and the exposure is reported promptly so testing and possible preventive treatment can begin within the recommended time. Caustic agents like bleach damage tissue and are not recommended.

questions.ref: NREMT EMT exam outline: Operations (ambulance operations, pediatric transport)
questions.q: How should a stable 3-year-old be secured for ambulance transport?
options: On a parent's lap on the bench seat
In a child restraint secured to the stretcher
Unrestrained on the stretcher mattress
Standing beside a parent holding a rail
questions.explain: Children are transported in a properly sized restraint system, such as a child restraint device secured to the stretcher. Holding a child on a lap is unsafe because an adult cannot hold a child in place during a crash or sudden stop.
